To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) spontaneous action potentials are necessary for the development of normal cortical networks, (2) homeostatic regulation of SAP activity protects developing networks from hyperactivity, (3) the protective effect of homeostatically regulated SAP activity is proportional to its level, and (4) GABAergic inhibition is not sufficient to prevent the development and persistence of network hyperactivity during development

(1) the homeostatic regulation of spontaneous neuronal firing patterns is not a general phenomenon, but depends on the particular culture conditions used; and (2) the degree to which the homeostatic response is successful depends upon the degree to which SAP firing patterns approximate those observed under normal conditions.

the homeostatic control of spontaneous firing in developing neocortex is not a general property of the isolated cortex culture preparation but is instead a property of the intact brain, as shown by our co-culture experiments, and that the homeostatically regulated firing patterns in developing neocortical networks are not only a property of the isolated culture preparation but are also a property of the developing brain, as shown both by our co-cultures and by our earlier experiments using isolated cultures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
homeostatic regulation of spontaneous neuronal activity during the early stages of cortical development.
the question of how homeostatic regulation of neuronal excitability is achieved.
the role of homeostatic regulation of synaptic transmission in normal cortical development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

SAP activity, in the context of co-cultures of neonatal neocortex, is not only a necessary but also a sufficient precondition for homeostatic protection against the development of epileptiform network hyperactivity.
homeostatic regulation of spontaneous neuronal activity can protect developing cerebral cortex from becoming hyperactive, provided that the excitatory synaptic input is not completely blocked.
SAP activity in co-cultures is less vulnerable to the loss of synaptic drive, while paroxysmal firing is less vulnerable in isolated cultures, than previously thought.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

homeostatic mechanisms can prevent the development of hyperexcitable networks even in the absence of synaptic transmission, provided that spontaneous firing activity is not completely suppressed during the period of chronic treatment.

homeostatic mechanisms are not able to prevent the development and expression of hyperexcitability in neocortial networks, but that they can prevent the development of hyperexcitablity when the network is not too far from its normal level of activity.

the homeostatic response of cortical neurons to chronic suppression of synaptic activity is not a general property of the cortex, but is rather dependent on the particular culture conditions and the degree to which these conditions allow for the development of normal synaptic connectivity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
spontaneous neuronal activity plays a key role in shaping the development of neocortical networks.
the development of cortical network excitability depends on the balance of spontaneous and evoked activity in the network.
homeostatic plasticity is a robust and powerful phenomenon, but its expression depends on the precise nature of the perturbations that trigger it.
